ECE 6612

Authenticated encryption

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how a receiver verifies a protected message before releasing its plaintext

Authenticated encryption with associated data takes a secret key K, nonce N, plaintext P, and associated data A. It protects P while binding the visible context A to that protected message. The diagram shows the authentication tag separately; an algorithm may encode it inside its ciphertext output.

Authenticated decryption returns plaintext or failure. The receiver releases plaintext only after successful verification. For a nonce-based mode such as AES-GCM, encryption nonces must be unique for a given key; secrecy of the nonce is unnecessary.

Message authentication and replay policy have separate jobs. A previously valid packet can still be a replay, so the surrounding protocol must enforce its sequence or freshness rules. A handshake can bind the symmetric key to an intended peer identity.

Example

A record can encrypt a sensor reading while authenticating a visible sequence field. Altering that field changes the verification input, so the original tag will not validate the modified record except with the algorithm's small forgery probability.

Sources and scope
  • RFC 5116: AEAD interface and nonce requirements
  • RFC 8446: TLS 1.3 record protection

Practice

1. Does a valid authentication tag alone establish that a packet is fresh?

Consider an unchanged copy of a previously valid packet.

The copied packet can still verify. The protocol must separately check freshness, such as whether an authenticated sequence number has already been accepted.
